summary: Liberian President Charles Taylor blamed rebels in neighbouring Guinea for a cross-border raid on Lofa county, declared a state of emergency, closed Liberia's borders, and ordered a general mobilisation.
Liberian President Charles Taylor calls in Sierra Leonean Revolutionary United Front guerrillas to help fight an insurgency threatening his rule.
Rebels fought their way to the outskirts of Monrovia in a renewed effort to oust President Charles Taylor.
Charles Taylor was charged with war crimes and crimes against humanity by a UN-backed tribunal investigating Sierra Leone's war.
Charles Taylor was indicted by Sierra Leone's UN-backed war crimes court for his part in the Sierra Leone atrocities.
Charles Taylor declared his defiance as rebel fighters from the Liberians United for Reconciliation and Democracy closed in on the centre of Monrovia, Liberia.
Rebel fighters encircled Monrovia and gave Liberian President Charles Taylor 72 hours to step down.
Rebels advanced into Monrovia, threatening Charles Taylor’s rule as civilians fled and Taylor vowed to remain in power.
Liberian President Charles Taylor renewed his promise to step aside and seek asylum in Nigeria, stating he would only relinquish power when an international force arrived.
Liberian President Charles Taylor accepted an offer of asylum in Nigeria but gave no indication of when he would leave, insisting on an orderly exit from power.
The Archbishop of Monrovia warns that the ceasefire between rebel forces and militia backing President Charles Taylor is in imminent danger of breaking down.
Liberian President Charles Taylor said he would step down and take up Nigeria's offer of asylum as rebels pressed a third assault on Monrovia.

West African leaders called for the deployment of a Nigerian vanguard peacekeeping force to Liberia by Monday at the latest and for the departure of President Charles Taylor within three days of that.

Liberian President Charles Taylor agreed to leave the country on Monday and accept asylum in Nigeria, though a Western diplomat said he was suggesting he might stay and rule behind the scenes after installing a crony as president.
Liberia asked the International Court of Justice to block Sierra Leone’s war crimes indictment and arrest warrant against President Charles Taylor, arguing he has head-of-state immunity.
Liberian President Charles Taylor is due to resign and cede power, with his exile to Nigeria being arranged.
Liberian President Charles Taylor has agreed to step down and accept asylum in Nigeria, though his promise was conditional and it remained uncertain whether he would cede power by that date.
Charles Taylor stepped down as president of Liberia and flew into exile in Nigeria.
Liberian rebel groups signed a peace accord with government officials to end their three-year insurgency, a week after forcing warlord Charles Taylor into exile.
Nigeria’s president Olusegun Obasanjo and Liberia’s president Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf agree to send former Liberian dictator Charles Taylor to face trial before the UN special court in Sierra Leone.
The new Liberian government of President Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf formally requested the extradition of former president Charles Taylor from Nigeria back to Liberia.
Nigeria confirmed it had received a request from the Liberian government to extradite former Liberian president Charles Taylor to face war crimes charges.
UN war crimes tribunal prosecutor Desmond de Silva asks Nigeria's president Olusegun Obasanjo to arrest former Liberian president Charles Taylor, amid concerns he might flee to evade trial.
Nigeria said Liberia's new government, which had formally sought Charles Taylor's extradition, was free to take him into custody, though it did not say when or how he would be transferred.
Charles Taylor disappeared from his safe haven in Nigeria days before he was due to be transferred to a war crimes court.

Charles Taylor was locked up in a cell of the United Nations special tribunal on war crimes in Sierra Leone, and the tribunal asked for him to be taken to the special international war crimes court in the Hague.
Former Liberian president Charles Taylor appeared before a UN-backed war crimes court in Freetown, Sierra Leone, and pleaded not guilty to 11 charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity.
The international community is working to move former Liberian president Charles Taylor's war crimes trial to The Hague, though Taylor has asked for the case to remain in Sierra Leone.
Britain and the US plan to move the war crimes trial of former Liberian President Charles Taylor from Freetown to The Hague, prompting growing anger in Sierra Leone.
The British government offers to imprison former Liberian president Charles Taylor if he is found guilty of war crimes, breaking an international deadlock over his trial.
The UK foreign secretary announced that former Liberian president Charles Taylor could serve any sentence in the UK if convicted of war crimes by a UN-backed court.
Charles Taylor, the former president of Liberia, was transferred to The Hague to face a war crimes trial related to Sierra Leone's civil war.
Former Liberian president Charles Taylor was transferred to The Hague to face war-crimes charges related to Sierra Leone's civil war.
Charles Taylor becomes the first African head of state to go on trial for serious crimes before an international criminal court.
Charles Taylor failed to appear at the start of his war crimes trial in The Hague, and his British lawyer walked out after a row with the presiding judge.
The trial of former Liberian president Charles Taylor opens at The Hague, where he is accused of war crimes during the diamond-fuelled conflict in neighbouring Sierra Leone.

Former Liberian president Charles Taylor appeared in court for the first time since the start of his trial for alleged atrocities during Sierra Leone's civil war, ending his boycott and pleading not guilty to a slightly amended charge of sexual slavery.
The prosecutor in the special Sierra Leone tribunal said he was optimistic that Charles Taylor's war crimes trial will proceed on schedule despite recent delays.
Judges agreed to delay until January the war crimes trial of former Liberian president Charles Taylor at The Hague.
The war crimes trial of former Liberian president Charles Taylor began at a special tribunal in The Hague, where he pleaded innocent to 11 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity.
The war crimes trial of former Liberian president Charles Taylor reopened at the International Criminal Court in The Hague, six months after he boycotted the opening session.
A survivor testified at the international war crimes trial of former Liberian president Charles Taylor in The Hague, describing atrocities committed during the Sierra Leone civil war.
A commander in Charles Taylor's militia testified at Taylor's war crimes trial that Taylor ordered fighters to eat their enemies, including UN peacekeepers, as a means of terrorizing the population.
The torture trial of Charles Taylor Jr., son of former Liberian president Charles Taylor, began in Miami, marking the first US prosecution of torture committed in a foreign country.
Charles Taylor's son, Charles "Chuckie" Taylor Jr., was sentenced to 97 years in prison in the US for torture committed in Liberia.
The chief prosecutor of the Special Court for Sierra Leone warns that Charles Taylor could be set free if the court runs out of funding due to the global economic crisis.
Lawyers for former Liberian president Charles Taylor began his war crimes defence at The Hague, arguing he was not responsible for atrocities committed by rebels in Sierra Leone.
Former Liberian president Charles Taylor launched his own defence at his war crimes trial, dismissing charges of murder and crimes against humanity as based on lies and misinformation.

Former Liberian president Charles Taylor testified at his war crimes trial that he was indicted as part of a US "regime change" plan and claimed he was duped by Nigeria into being arrested there in 2006.

Special Court for Sierra Leone prosecutor Stephen Rapp suggested Charles Taylor may go free because of budgetary reasons, raising concern within the Liberian government and emboldening Taylor supporters.
UN war crimes prosecutors in The Hague called for Naomi Campbell to be compelled to testify over claims that she was given "blood diamonds" by Liberia's former president Charles Taylor.
The Special Court for Sierra Leone granted prosecutors' request to summon Naomi Campbell to give evidence in the war crimes trial of former Liberian president Charles Taylor.
Naomi Campbell is granted special protection by a UN war crimes tribunal for her testimony over claims she was given a blood diamond by Charles Taylor.
Naomi Campbell testified at Charles Taylor's war crimes trial at The Hague, saying she received "dirty-looking stones" but not stating that Taylor gave her diamonds.

Naomi Campbell's former agent Carole White testified at Charles Taylor's war crimes tribunal, but during cross-examination she admitted parts of her evidence linking Taylor to a gift of diamonds were mistaken or based on her own assumptions, and the defense branded her account "a complete pack of lies."
Mia Farrow testifies at Charles Taylor's war crimes trial that Naomi Campbell told her Taylor had sent Campbell a large diamond.

Two witnesses in the trial of ex-Liberian President Charles Taylor testified that the model Naomi Campbell received diamonds from Liberian warlord Charles Taylor, contradicting Campbell's earlier testimony.
WikiLeaks cables reveal US concerns that judges in Charles Taylor's war crimes trial at The Hague have deliberately slowed proceedings, with US officials exploring options to try him in the US.
Charles Taylor's lead defence lawyer Courtenay Griffiths stormed out of the war crimes trial in The Hague after judges refused to accept a written summary of Taylor's defence.
Former Liberian president Charles Taylor is due to appear at a war crimes court in The Hague to hear verdicts on 11 charges, with the UK having offered prison space if he is convicted.

Naomi Campbell testified at Charles Taylor's war crimes trial that she received a pouch of uncut diamonds after a 1997 dinner also attended by Taylor, while Mia Farrow contradicted aspects of her testimony.
Former Liberian president Charles Taylor was found guilty by a UN-backed court of aiding and abetting war crimes and crimes against humanity in Sierra Leone.
Charles Taylor was found guilty at The Hague of aiding and abetting war crimes in Sierra Leone.

UN prosecutors urged the Special Court for Sierra Leone to sentence former Liberian president Charles Taylor to 80 years in prison for aiding and abetting war crimes and crimes against humanity, with sentencing scheduled for 2012-05-30.
Former Liberian president Charles Taylor is scheduled to be sentenced by the Special Court for Sierra Leone for aiding and abetting war crimes during the Sierra Leone civil war.
Charles Taylor loses appeal at The Hague over war crimes conviction.
The UK Ministry of Justice confirms that convicted former Liberian president Charles Taylor will serve his 50-year sentence for war crimes in a British prison.
Charles Taylor launches a legal action at the UN-backed tribunal in The Hague seeking removal from a British prison to an African jail, arguing he is deprived of his right to family life.
Agnes Reeves Taylor, the ex-wife of former Liberian president Charles Taylor, was charged with four torture offences allegedly committed between 1989 and 1991.
Charles Taylor's war crimes trial is mentioned, with him reportedly saying he will prove his innocence.
Charles Taylor was found guilty of war crimes in Sierra Leone.
Charles Taylor speaks at sentencing for Sierra Leone war crimes.
Defence and prosecution lawyers react to the sentence in the Charles Taylor trial.
